problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=2{x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=3{x}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs above, where $t\in R.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.$\,$ The function $a(t)=[\begin{aligned}4{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ 
{{field-1}} 
a solution of the system.

$\,$ The function $b(t)=[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{3t} \\ 2{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}]$ 
{{field-2}} 
a solution of the system.

$\,$ The function $c(t)=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}]$ 
{{field-3}} 
a solution of the system.

$\,$ {{field-4}} 
is a set of fundamental solutions to the system because the Wronskian 

$$
W({{field-5}})={{field-6}}\ne 0
$$

$\,$ for at least one $t\in R.$
worked_solution:
The Wronskian $W({x}_{1},{x}_{2})$ of two vector-valued functions 

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{11}(t) \\ {x}_{21}(t)\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{12}(t) \\ {x}_{22}(t)\end{aligned}]
$$

is defined as

$$
W({x}_{1},{x}_{2})=det({x}_{1},{x}_{2})=|\begin{aligned}{x}_{11}(t) & {x}_{12}(t) \\ {x}_{21}(t) & {x}_{22}(t)\end{aligned}|.
$$

Note the following:

- If the Wronskian is not identically zero, then ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are linearly independent.

- If the Wronskian is identically zero, and it's known that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are solutions to the same system of linear ODEs, then ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are linearly dependent.

First, we write our system in matrix form:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

Now, let's substitute the given vectors into the matrix differential equation:

- $a(t)=[\begin{aligned}4{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ $\text{is}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}(4{e}^{2t})^{′} \\ (0)^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}8{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot 4{e}^{2t}+1\cdot 0 \\ 0\cdot 4{e}^{2t}+3\cdot 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}8{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}8{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- $b(t)=[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{3t} \\ 2{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}]$ $\text{is}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}(2{e}^{3t})^{′} \\ (2{e}^{3t})^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2{e}^{3t} \\ 2{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}6{e}^{3t} \\ 6{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot 2{e}^{3t}+1\cdot 2{e}^{3t} \\ 0\cdot 2{e}^{3t}+3\cdot 2{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}6{e}^{3t} \\ 6{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}6{e}^{3t} \\ 6{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}]\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- $c(t)=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}]$ $\text{isn't}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}({e}^{2t})^{′} \\ ({e}^{2t})^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2{e}^{2t} \\ 2{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot {e}^{2t}+1\cdot {e}^{2t} \\ 0\cdot {e}^{2t}+3\cdot {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2{e}^{2t} \\ 2{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{2t} \\ 3{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}]\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Now, consider the set of solutions ${a,b}.$ Its Wronskian is

$$
\begin{aligned}W(a,b) & =|\begin{aligned}4{e}^{2t} & 2{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & 2{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}| \\  & =(4{e}^{2t})\cdot 2{e}^{3t}-(2{e}^{3t})\cdot 0 \\  & =8{e}^{5t}-0 \\  & =8{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}
$$

which is nonzero for at least one $t\in R.$ Thus, since $a$ and $b$ are both solutions of the same linear system, and their Wronskian is nonzero for at least one $t\in R,$ ${a,b}$ is a set of fundamental solutions of the system.
